scenes.visual: tree drops leaves, pile stacks higher each year, question appears
scenes.tts: In autumn, many Virginia trees drop their leaves onto the forest floor. Leaves fall every year. If nothing happened to them, the layers would stack higher and higher. So where do all the fallen leaves go? What would happen if nothing broke them down?
scenes.narration: In autumn, many Virginia trees drop their leaves onto the forest floor. Leaves fall every year. If nothing happened to them, the layers would stack higher and higher. So where do all the fallen leaves go? What would happen if nothing broke them down?

scenes.visual: sun to tree to sugar (producer); acorns to deer (consumer)
scenes.tts: Ecologists sort the living things in a forest by three main jobs. A producer captures energy from sunlight and stores it in sugar, also called glucose. Trees, grasses and mosses are producers. A consumer gets energy by eating other organisms. A deer eating acorns is a consumer.
scenes.narration: Ecologists sort the living things in a forest by three main jobs. A producer captures energy from sunlight and stores it in sugar, also called glucose. Trees, grasses and mosses are producers. A consumer gets energy by eating other organisms. A deer eating acorns is a consumer.

scenes.visual: dead matter to decomposers (fungi, bacteria); fungus releases chemicals outside its body, leaf breaks, pieces taken in; worms tear leaf into bits
scenes.tts: A decomposer breaks down dead plants, dead animals and wastes. The main decomposers are fungi and bacteria. A fungus has no mouth. It releases chemicals that break down the leaf outside its body. Then it takes in the small pieces. Worms and millipedes help by tearing dead leaves into smaller bits.

scenes.visual: leaf broken down, nutrients appear in soil, roots take them up, carbon dioxide rises to the air
scenes.tts: As decomposers break down a leaf, nutrients go back into the soil. A nutrient is a substance, such as nitrogen, that living things need to grow. Plant roots take up those nutrients and use them again. Some of the leaf's carbon goes into the air as carbon dioxide, released by decomposers.

scenes.visual: decomposers removed: leaves pile up, fewer nutrients, plants may grow less; then the three groups linked
scenes.tts: Now take the decomposers away. Dead leaves would pile up. Fewer nutrients would return to the soil, so plants may grow less over time. Producers, consumers and decomposers are linked. A change in one group can reach the others.
scenes.narration: Now take the decomposers away. Dead leaves would pile up. Fewer nutrients would return to the soil, so plants may grow less over time. Producers, consumers and decomposers are linked. A change in one group can reach the others.

scenes.visual: matter loop with a moving dot; energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat; the answer
scenes.tts: Matter goes around and around. Energy does not. Energy enters as sunlight and leaves as heat. So where do the fallen leaves go? Fungi, bacteria and small animals mostly break them down, and the nutrients go back into the soil, where trees take them up again.
